corpusNote: Plato's is the first philosophical corpus to survive complete: not a single dialogue accepted as genuinely his has been lost. The ancient edition, arranged by Thrasyllus (1st c. CE) into nine tetralogies of four works each — 36 titles — is the corpus we still print. The scholarly questions are therefore not survival but (1) authenticity at the edges (several tetralogy works are now judged spurious), (2) chronology (the early/middle/late grouping that underwrites almost all interpretation is a modern stylometric reconstruction, not an ancient datum), and (3) the 'unwritten doctrines' — the tradition, resting on Aristotle and the Seventh Letter, that Plato reserved his deepest teaching for oral discussion in the Academy.

referenceSystems.name: Stephanus pagination
referenceSystems.note: The universal citation system for Plato, from Henri Estienne's 1578 edition — e.g. Republic 514a. Every modern edition and translation carries Stephanus numbers in the margin; cite Plato by these, never by page of a particular translation.

referenceSystems.name: Thrasyllan tetralogies
referenceSystems.note: The 9×4 arrangement in Diogenes Laertius III.56–62, the basis of the transmitted corpus and of the OCT/Burnet edition order.

referenceSystems.name: Oxford Classical Texts (Burnet)
referenceSystems.note: Burnet, Platonis Opera, 5 vols. (1900–1907); the standard Greek text, now being replaced volume by volume (Duke et al., vol. I, 1995).

works.title: Euthyphro
works.transmission: Full medieval manuscript tradition (principal witnesses: Clarkianus B, Venetus T, Vindobonensis W).
works.summary: On the eve of Socrates' own trial, he questions Euthyphro, who is prosecuting his father for impiety, about the definition of piety (to hosion). The 'Euthyphro dilemma': is the pious loved by the gods because it is pious, or pious because it is loved? Ends in aporia.
editions: Duke et al., OCT vol. I (1995)
translations: Grube (rev. Cooper), in Plato: Complete Works (1997)

works.title: Apology of Socrates
works.authenticity: Genuine, undisputed. Not a dialogue but Plato's version of Socrates' defence speech at his trial in 399 BCE.
works.summary: Socrates' defence against the charges of impiety and corrupting the youth: the Delphic oracle and his mission of examination; 'the unexamined life is not worth living' (38a); the refusal to cease philosophising; the counter-penalty; the closing address to the jurors on death. The founding text of philosophy as a way of life and of intellectual martyrdom.
editions: Duke et al., OCT vol. I (1995)

works.title: Crito
works.summary: In prison, Socrates refuses Crito's offer of escape. The personified Laws of Athens argue that citizenship is a tacit contract and that to flee would be to injure the city that raised him. The classic statement of the duty to obey the law and the wrong of returning injustice for injustice.
editions: Duke et al., OCT vol. I (1995)

works.title: Phaedo
works.summary: Socrates' last conversation and death: four arguments for the immortality of the soul (the cyclical, the recollection, the affinity, and the final argument from the Form of Life), the theory of Forms as the objects of true knowledge, philosophy as 'practice for death', and the myth of the soul's judgement. Closes with the drinking of the hemlock.
editions: Duke et al., OCT vol. I (1995)

works.title: Cratylus
works.summary: On the correctness of names: are names conventional (Hermogenes) or natural, fitting their objects (Cratylus)? Socrates' long etymologies, the critique of Heraclitean flux as a basis for language, and the conclusion that knowledge must reach things themselves, not through names. Plato's philosophy of language.
editions: Duke et al., OCT vol. I (1995)

works.title: Theaetetus
works.transmission: Full manuscript tradition; a papyrus commentary (the Anonymous Theaetetus Commentary) also survives.
works.summary: What is knowledge (epistēmē)? Three definitions tested and rejected: knowledge as perception (with Protagoras' 'man the measure' and the Heraclitean flux), as true belief, and as true belief with an account (logos). The 'midwife' image of Socratic method; the Digression on the philosopher; ends in aporia. Foundational for epistemology.
editions: Duke et al., OCT vol. I (1995)

works.title: Sophist
works.summary: The Eleatic Visitor, not Socrates, leads. The method of division (diairesis) to define the sophist; the 'parricide' of Parmenides — establishing that not-being in the sense of difference does exist, so false statement is possible; the communion of kinds (Being, Sameness, Difference, Motion, Rest). Central to Plato's late metaphysics and logic.
editions: Duke et al., OCT vol. I (1995)

works.title: Statesman (Politicus)
works.summary: Sequel to the Sophist: defining the statesman by division; the myth of the reversed cosmos; the art of statesmanship as the weaving together of the citizens' characters; the ranking of constitutions and the rule of the expert above written law. The bridge between the Republic and the Laws.
editions: Duke et al., OCT vol. I (1995)

works.title: Parmenides
works.transmission: Full manuscript tradition; central to the Neoplatonic curriculum (Proclus' vast commentary survives).
works.summary: The aged Parmenides criticises the young Socrates' Theory of Forms (the Third Man regress, the separation problem), then demonstrates dialectical method through eight (or nine) deductions about 'the One' — whether it is or is not, and the consequences. Plato's most difficult work and the seedbed of Neoplatonism.

works.title: Philebus
works.summary: Is the good life one of pleasure or of wisdom? The fourfold division of all being (limit, unlimited, mixture, cause); the analysis of true and false pleasures; the final ranking, in which neither pleasure nor intellect alone but a measured mixture, with measure and proportion highest, constitutes the good. Plato's fullest treatment of pleasure and the closest link to the 'unwritten' metaphysics of limit and the unlimited.
translations: Frede, in Complete Works (1997); Gosling (Clarendon Plato, 1975)

works.title: Symposium
works.summary: Seven speeches on erōs at a drinking party: culminating in Socrates' report of Diotima's teaching — the ascent from love of one beautiful body to the Form of Beauty itself — and Alcibiades' drunken encomium of Socrates. The classic text on love, beauty, and philosophical desire.

works.title: Phaedrus
works.summary: On love, the soul, and rhetoric: the myth of the soul as charioteer with two horses; love as divine madness and the recollection of Beauty; the requirements of a true (philosophical) rhetoric; and the closing critique of writing — the story of Theuth and Thamus, and why the written word cannot defend itself or teach. The key text for Plato's view of his own medium.
translations: Nehamas & Woodruff, in Complete Works (1997); Rowe (1986)

works.title: Alcibiades I (Alcibiades Major)
works.transmission: Full manuscript tradition; in antiquity it was the standard first text of the Neoplatonic Plato curriculum.
works.authenticity: Disputed. Antiquity accepted it as genuine and foundational; the 19th century (Schleiermacher) rejected it; recent scholarship (Denyer 2001) has substantially rehabilitated it. Treat as doubtful-leaning-genuine.
works.summary: Socrates turns the ambitious young Alcibiades toward self-knowledge: 'know thyself' means know the soul, and one cannot govern others without first governing oneself. The soul as the true self, seen reflected in another soul. Whether or not by Plato, the most influential ancient statement of the care-of-the-self theme.

works.title: Alcibiades II (Alcibiades Minor)
works.transmission: Full manuscript tradition, but on a shorter and later stemma.
works.authenticity: Spurious by near-consensus. On prayer — that one should not pray for things without knowledge, since one may pray for one's own harm.
works.summary: A short dialogue arguing that ignorance makes prayer dangerous. Stylistically un-Platonic; probably a 3rd-century Academic exercise.
translations: Hutchinson, in Complete Works (1997), which prints it among the works 'now generally believed not to be by Plato'

works.title: Hipparchus
works.authenticity: Spurious by wide consensus. On the love of gain (philokerdeia).
works.summary: Short dialogue on whether the love of gain is bad and whether all men love gain; includes a digression on the tyrant Hipparchus. Un-Platonic in argument and style.

works.title: Rival Lovers (Lovers / Amatores)
works.authenticity: Spurious by wide consensus. On whether philosophy is beneficial and what it is.
works.summary: Socrates questions two young men, one athletic and one intellectual, about the value of philosophy, arguing it is not polymathy but a kind of measured knowledge. Probably an Academic composition.

works.title: Theages
works.authenticity: Spurious by wide consensus, though valued for its detailed account of Socrates' daimonion.
works.summary: On whether wisdom can be taught and on association with Socrates; notable for its treatment of the divine sign as conferring benefit on Socrates' companions.

works.title: Charmides
works.summary: On sōphrosynē (temperance/self-control/soundness of mind): successive definitions — quietness, modesty, doing one's own, self-knowledge, knowledge of knowledge — all found wanting. Ends in aporia. Features the young Charmides and Critias, later of the Thirty Tyrants.

works.title: Laches
works.summary: On courage (andreia): the generals Laches and Nicias offer definitions — standing firm, and knowledge of the fearful and hopeful — each refuted. Raises whether virtue is one or many and whether it can be taught. Ends in aporia.

works.title: Lysis
works.summary: On philia (friendship/love): what makes one a friend, whether like is friend to like or opposite to opposite, and the notion of a 'first friend' for whose sake all else is dear. Ends in aporia. Plato's companion to the Symposium on the nature of attachment.

works.title: Euthydemus
works.summary: Socrates contrasts genuine philosophical protreptic with the fallacious 'eristic' of two sophist brothers, whose logical tricks are displayed and dissected. A comic but serious study of sophistry, ambiguity, and the exhortation to virtue.

works.title: Protagoras
works.summary: Socrates debates the great sophist Protagoras on whether virtue can be taught and whether the virtues are one. Protagoras' Great Speech (the myth of Prometheus and the origin of political art); the interpretation of a poem by Simonides; and the closing argument that virtue is knowledge and courage a form of it — with the famous 'hedonic calculus' and the denial of akrasia.
translations: Lombardo & Bell, in Complete Works (1997); Taylor (Clarendon Plato, 1976)

works.title: Gorgias
works.summary: On rhetoric, power, and justice: against Gorgias, Polus, and Callicles, Socrates argues that rhetoric is mere flattery, that it is better to suffer wrong than to do it, that the tyrant is wretched, and that a well-ordered soul matters more than worldly power. Callicles' defence of the natural right of the strong is the most powerful anti-Socratic voice in Plato. Ends with the myth of judgement.
translations: Zeyl, in Complete Works (1997); Irwin (Clarendon Plato, 1979)

works.title: Meno
works.summary: Can virtue be taught? Introduces the theory of recollection (anamnesis) via the slave-boy's geometry demonstration, the method of hypothesis, and Meno's Paradox of inquiry (how can you seek what you don't know?). Distinguishes knowledge from true belief. Transitional between Socratic and Platonic phases.

works.title: Hippias Major (Greater Hippias)
works.authenticity: Disputed; long doubted but now often defended as genuine (Woodruff). On the definition of the fine/beautiful (to kalon).
works.summary: Socrates and the sophist Hippias seek to define the kalon (the fine, beautiful, admirable): the appropriate, the useful, the beneficial, the pleasant through sight and hearing — each rejected. A model aporetic dialogue, whether or not Plato's.

works.title: Hippias Minor (Lesser Hippias)
citations: DL III.59; cited by Aristotle, Metaphysics 1025a
works.transmission: Full manuscript tradition; attested by Aristotle, which secures its authenticity.
works.authenticity: Genuine — Aristotle refers to its argument, which few other dialogues in this tetralogy can claim.
works.summary: The paradox that the person who does wrong voluntarily (the one who can err deliberately) is 'better' than the one who errs involuntarily — a deliberately unsettling argument about knowledge, ability, and the voluntariness of wrongdoing.

works.title: Ion
works.summary: Socrates questions the rhapsode Ion: poetic and performative excellence is not a technē (craft-knowledge) but divine inspiration, the poet a magnet transmitting the Muse's power through a chain of rings. Plato's first statement on inspiration and the epistemic poverty of poetry.

works.title: Menexenus
citations: DL III.60; cited by Aristotle, Rhetoric 1367b
works.transmission: Full manuscript tradition; referred to by Aristotle.
works.authenticity: Genuine — attested by Aristotle, despite the puzzle of Socrates delivering a speech about events after his death.
works.summary: Socrates recites a funeral oration he attributes to Aspasia, parodying Athenian patriotic rhetoric. A satirical companion to the Gorgias' critique of oratory; its anachronisms are part of the joke.

works.title: Clitophon
works.extent: Complete but very short. Tetralogy VIII.1. Stephanus 406a–410e.
works.authenticity: Disputed; leans spurious, but taken seriously as a critique of Socratic protreptic. The only dialogue in which Socrates is criticised and does not reply.
works.summary: Clitophon complains that Socrates is superb at exhorting people to pursue virtue but never says what justice actually is or how to attain it — a pointed critique of the aporetic method, prefacing the Republic in the tetralogy.

works.title: Republic
works.extent: Complete, in 10 books. Tetralogy VIII.2. Stephanus 327a–621d.
works.transmission: Full manuscript tradition; the most read of Plato's works from antiquity onward. Portions on papyrus (incl. the Oxyrhynchus finds).
works.summary: What is justice, and is the just life happier than the unjust? Building an ideal city to see justice 'writ large': the three classes and three parts of the soul; the education of the guardians; the community of women, children, and property; the philosopher-kings; the Theory of Forms and the Form of the Good; the three great images (Sun, Divided Line, Cave); the critique of poetry and of imitation; the decline of constitutions; and the closing Myth of Er on the soul's immortality and choice of lives.
translations: Grube (rev. Reeve), in Complete Works (1997); Bloom (1968)

works.title: Timaeus
works.transmission: Full manuscript tradition; through Calcidius' partial Latin translation it was the only Plato known to the Latin Middle Ages, making it his most historically influential work.
works.summary: The cosmos as the work of a divine craftsman (the Demiurge) shaping the receptacle (chōra) according to the eternal Forms: the World-Soul, the mathematical structure of the four elements (the Platonic solids), time as 'the moving image of eternity', the mechanics of perception, physiology, and disease. Plato's physics and cosmology.
translations: Zeyl, in Complete Works (1997); Cornford, Plato's Cosmology (1937)

works.title: Critias
works.extent: Incomplete — breaks off mid-sentence. Tetralogy VIII.4. Stephanus 106a–121c.
works.transmission: Full manuscript tradition; the text simply stops, apparently never finished by Plato.
works.summary: Sequel to the Timaeus: the myth of Atlantis and its war with primeval Athens nine thousand years before. The description of Atlantis' geography and constitution breaks off just as Zeus prepares to address the gods. The source of the entire Atlantis tradition.

works.title: Minos
works.authenticity: Spurious by wide consensus; probably an Academic work prefacing the Laws in the tetralogy.
works.summary: On what law is — 'the discovery of what is', and on Minos as the model lawgiver. Serves as an introduction to the Laws.

works.title: Laws

date.note: Plato's last work, left unrevised at his death; reportedly transcribed from wax by Philip of Opus.

works.extent: Complete, in 12 books — Plato's longest work. Tetralogy IX.2. Stephanus 624a–969d.
works.transmission: Full manuscript tradition; Diogenes Laertius (III.37) reports it was left 'in the wax' and copied out by Philip of Opus.
works.authenticity: Genuine, undisputed, though its final editing was posthumous.
works.summary: Three old men design the laws of a new Cretan colony, Magnesia — a 'second-best' state more practicable than the Republic's. Detailed legislation on marriage, education, property, religion, and punishment; the preludes to laws; the Nocturnal Council; and in Book X the first sustained philosophical argument for the existence of gods and against atheism, grounded in soul as self-motion. The foundational text of philosophy of law.

works.title: Epinomis
works.authenticity: Spurious by wide consensus; usually attributed to Philip of Opus, the editor of the Laws, as its appendix.
works.summary: An appendix to the Laws on the highest wisdom: astronomy and the mathematical sciences as the true path to virtue and the knowledge of the divine cosmos. A key document of early Academy astral theology, whoever wrote it.
editions: Tarán, Academica: Plato, Philip of Opus, and the Pseudo-Platonic Epinomis (1975)
translations: McKirahan, in Complete Works (1997), among the spuria

works.title: Letters (Epistles)

date.note: Purported dates; several are certainly later forgeries.

works.extent: Thirteen letters. Tetralogy IX.4. Numbered I–XIII; cited by letter and Stephanus page (vol. III of Stephanus).
works.transmission: Transmitted as a collection within the corpus.
works.authenticity: Mixed and heavily disputed. Most are widely judged spurious. The Seventh Letter is the great exception — many (not all) scholars accept it as genuine or as an early authentic document; it is the single most important source for Plato's biography, his disastrous involvement in Syracusan politics under Dionysius II and Dion, and — crucially — for the 'unwritten doctrines', containing the famous 'philosophical digression' (341c–344d) arguing that the deepest truths cannot be put in writing at all. The Eighth is also sometimes defended.
works.summary: Autobiographical and political. Letter VII: the failure of the Sicilian project, the account of Plato's philosophical development, the digression on why he never wrote down his most serious teaching ('there neither is nor ever will be a treatise of mine on these matters'). The others range over Academy business, condolence, and financial affairs.
works.notes: The Seventh Letter's authenticity is one of the most consequential open questions in Plato scholarship — the entire 'esotericist' Tübingen reading (Krämer, Gaiser) leans on it plus Aristotle.

works.title: Appended spuria (Definitions, On Justice, On Virtue, Demodocus, Sisyphus, Halcyon, Eryxias, Axiochus, Epigrams)
works.extent: A group of short works transmitted with the corpus but outside the tetralogies; Diogenes Laertius III.62 already lists most as 'universally acknowledged spurious'.
works.transmission: Appended to the manuscript corpus after the tetralogies.
works.authenticity: Spurious by ancient and modern consensus. Diogenes names as agreed-spurious: Midon (or Horse-breeder), Eryxias (or Erasistratus), Alcyon, Acephali (Headless), Sisyphus, Axiochus, Phaeacians, Demodocus, Chelidon, Seventh Day, Epimenides. The Definitions (Horoi) — a lexicon of philosophical terms — and the Epigrams attributed to Plato also belong here.
works.summary: Academic and later exercises: the Definitions (a glossary), the pseudo-dialogues (Axiochus on the fear of death, Eryxias on wealth, Sisyphus on deliberation, Demodocus on giving advice), Halcyon (a fable, sometimes ascribed to Lucian), and the love-epigrams attributed to Plato (including the famous 'Aster' couplets), most of them Hellenistic.
editions: Burnet, OCT vol. V (Definitions and spuria)
translations: Cooper (ed.), Complete Works (1997), which prints the 'Spurious/Dubious' works in an appendix
works.notes: The Epigrams matter for the atlas as the only 'verse of Plato' students meet, though almost certainly not his.

works.title: The Unwritten Doctrines (agrapha dogmata)
works.extent: No text — an oral teaching reconstructed from Aristotle and the indirect tradition. Aristotle explicitly refers to Plato's 'so-called unwritten teachings' (agrapha dogmata, Physics 209b14–15).
citations: Aristoxenus, Elementa Harmonica II.30–31 (the lecture 'On the Good')
works.transmission: Aristotle, who spent twenty years in the Academy, reports doctrines found nowhere in the dialogues: the two highest principles, the One and the Indefinite Dyad (the Great-and-Small), from which the Forms and then numbers derive. Aristoxenus records the notorious public lecture 'On the Good' at which Plato's audience expected practical advice and got mathematics, concluding 'the Good is One'. The Tübingen–Milan school (Krämer, Gaiser, Reale) treats these as the true core of Platonism, of which the dialogues are only the outer, protreptic layer; the mainstream Anglophone tradition (Vlastos, Cherniss) is sceptical of reconstructing a systematic esoteric doctrine.
works.authenticity: Not a written work of Plato — the point is precisely that these teachings were, on this tradition, never written. Their content, extent, and even existence as a system are among the most contested questions in ancient philosophy.
works.summary: A principle-theory behind the Forms: the One (unity, limit, good) and the Indefinite Dyad (plurality, the unlimited) as the two ultimate sources; the Forms as Ideal Numbers generated from them; a hierarchy descending from principles to Forms to mathematicals to sensibles. The Philebus' limit/unlimited and the Timaeus' receptacle are read as the dialogues' nearest written approach to it.
editions: Gaiser, Platons ungeschriebene Lehre (1963) — collects the testimonia (Testimonia Platonica)
Krämer, Plato and the Foundations of Metaphysics (Eng. trans. 1990)
translations: Testimonia in Gaiser (1963); discussion in Reale, Toward a New Interpretation of Plato (Eng. 1997)
works.notes: Belongs in the atlas as the hinge between the written corpus and the Academy's oral life, and as the reason the Phaedrus' and Seventh Letter's critiques of writing are more than rhetorical.

works.title: Testimonia and biography (DL III; Academy tradition)
works.extent: Biographical and doctrinal reports on Plato and the early Academy.
citations: the Neoplatonic Prolegomena to Platonic Philosophy (Anon.)
the Academy tradition via Philodemus, Index Academicorum
works.transmission: Diogenes Laertius III is the fullest ancient Life; Philodemus' Herculaneum papyrus Index Academicorum preserves the Academy's institutional history; the Neoplatonists' introductory handbooks shaped the reading order.
works.authenticity: Not by Plato; the frame within which the corpus was read, ordered (the tetralogies themselves are here), and interpreted.
works.summary: Plato's life (Aristocles, called Plato; the three Sicilian voyages; the founding of the Academy c. 387 BCE), the ancient ordering debates (Aristophanes of Byzantium's trilogies vs Thrasyllus' tetralogies), and the doxographic summaries of 'Platonic doctrine'.
editions: Gaiser, Testimonia Platonica (in Platons ungeschriebene Lehre, 1963)
translations: Hicks, Diogenes Laertius, Loeb (1925) — public domain

excluded.title: Parmenides, Sophist, Statesman as works of the Eleatic philosophers
excluded.reason: These are Plato's dialogues named after or led by other philosophers, not works by them. A common cataloguing confusion (see the Parmenides file).

excluded.title: Halcyon
excluded.reason: Transmitted among Plato's spuria but also ascribed in antiquity to Leon of Byzantium or to Lucian.

sources: Diogenes Laertius, Lives III (Thrasyllan tetralogies, III.56–62)
Cooper (ed.), Plato: Complete Works (1997) — authenticity groupings
Aristotle, Metaphysics A.6 and M–N (unwritten doctrines)
